prompt: What does MongoDB store a document as on disk and on the wire?

choices.text: BSON, a binary encoding with more types than JSON has
choices.why: Right. Dates, 32- and 64-bit integers, Decimal128 and ObjectId are BSON types JSON lacks.

choices.text: JSON text, compressed
choices.why: mongosh prints something JSON-like, but the stored form is binary and typed.

choices.text: Rows of a hidden table, one column per field seen so far
choices.why: There is no table behind a collection; each document carries its own fields and types.

choices.text: JavaScript source code that mongosh evaluates when it reads
choices.why: mongosh speaks JavaScript; the server stores data, not programs.

prompt: In mongosh you insert `{ views: 12345678901 }`. What BSON type does `views` get?
hint: It does not fit in 32 bits.

choices.text: long, because the number is whole
choices.why: mongosh does not promote a large whole number to a 64-bit integer; that takes NumberLong.

choices.text: double
choices.why: Right. Only whole numbers that fit in 32 bits go as int; the rest are doubles, exact only up to 2^53.

choices.text: int, truncated to the largest 32-bit value
choices.why: Nothing is truncated; the value becomes a double.

choices.text: decimal, since doubles cannot hold eleven digits
choices.why: A double holds eleven digits exactly; decimal is used only when you ask for it.

prompt: Customer accounts get ObjectIds, and the account page's URL is `/account/<id>`. What does a stranger learn from one such URL?

choices.text: Nothing: the id is random from the first byte to the last, like a token
choices.why: Only five of the twelve bytes are random, and they are the same for every id from one process.

choices.text: The customer's e-mail, encoded in the middle bytes
choices.why: No field of the document goes into its ObjectId.

choices.text: Its creation time, to the second, and a guess at its neighbours
choices.why: Right. The timestamp is readable and the counter is sequential, so an ObjectId is no substitute for a random token.

choices.text: The server's address, which the client stamps in every id
choices.why: The 5-byte part is a random value per process, not an address.

prompt: How many bytes long is an ObjectId?
Why did `NumberDecimal(349.90 * 3)` give `Decimal128('1049.6999999999998')`?

choices.text: Decimal128 has too few digits for that value
choices.why: It has 34 significant digits; the error was already in its input.

choices.text: The multiplication ran as doubles before the decimal was built from the result
choices.why: Right. Build the decimal from a string, NumberDecimal("349.90"), and multiply on the server.

choices.text: The server rounds decimals to two places on insert
choices.why: Nothing was inserted, and the server does not round decimals that way.

choices.text: mongosh treats a decimal as a string until it is stored
choices.why: The value was a number when it reached NumberDecimal; that is what the warning was about.

prompt: An application runs `updateOne({ _id: orderId }, { $set: { status: "paid" } })` and treats the absence of an exception as success. What does it report when `orderId` names no order?
hint: Look at what the server answered for `_id: 22`.

choices.text: That it was paid: matchedCount 0 is not an error
choices.why: Right. An update that matches nothing is a successful update of nothing; the count is the only signal.

choices.text: An error, because the server refuses updates to missing documents
choices.why: The server raised nothing; it answered acknowledged: true.

choices.text: A new order, since updateOne inserts when nothing matches
choices.why: Only with upsert: true does an update insert.

choices.text: A timeout, while the server waits for the order to appear
choices.why: The server answers at once; it does not wait for a matching document.

prompt: Why was `updateOne({ _id: 1 }, { status: "shipped" })` refused?

choices.text: Order 1 had no status field yet
choices.why: It had one, and $set would create one anyway.

choices.text: Status changes need a multi-document transaction
choices.why: A single-document update is atomic without one.

choices.text: It had no `$` operator, so it would replace the whole order
choices.why: Right. Without the check it would mean replacing the order with { status: "shipped" } and losing the rest.

choices.text: `shipped` is not a value the collection's rules allow for status
choices.why: There was no validator on orders; the refusal came from mongosh itself.

prompt: A restocking job runs `updateOne({ _id: "LS-050" }, { $set: { name: "Laptop stand" }, $inc: { stock: 5 } }, { upsert: true })`. Its first attempt times out on the client, though the server applied it, and the job retries. What is the stock?
hint: The second call of the capture is this retry.

choices.text: 5, because an upsert is idempotent
choices.why: It is only idempotent with operators like $set; $inc adds again.
Right. The retry matched the document the first attempt created and added 5 again.

choices.text: An E11000 error, because the first attempt already inserted LS-050
choices.why: An upsert that finds the document updates it; only a plain insert collides.

choices.text: 0, since a timed-out write is rolled back by the server
choices.why: The server does not know the client gave up; the write stays.

prompt: Two clients run `updateOne({ _id: "MN-330" }, { $inc: { stock: -1 } })` at the same moment, with stock at 1. What is the stock afterwards?

choices.text: 0, because the second decrement read the old value
choices.why: That is what read-subtract-write in the application does; $inc is applied by the server to the current value.
Right. Each $inc is atomic on the document; preventing a negative needs a filter such as stock: { $gt: 0 }.

choices.text: 1, because conflicting updates cancel each other
choices.why: Neither update is cancelled; both are applied, one after the other.

choices.text: An error for one of them, since stock cannot go below zero
choices.why: Nothing forbade a negative stock; a validator with minimum: 0 would, and the validation section adds one.

prompt: Complete the filter that finds the orders with a line for the cable: `db.orders.find({ "___": "CB-012" })`.
hint: A dotted path into the array of lines.

prompt: `db.products.insertOne({ _id: "KB-101", ... })` is refused with E11000. What enforced it?

choices.text: A validator the products collection was created with
choices.why: No validator existed yet; E11000 is a duplicate key, not a failed rule.

choices.text: The unique index on `_id` every collection has
choices.why: Right. It cannot be dropped, and it is the one constraint MongoDB enforces unasked.

choices.text: mongosh, which remembers the ids it has inserted
choices.why: A new mongosh session was refused just the same; the check is on the server.

choices.text: A foreign key from orders to products
choices.why: MongoDB has no foreign keys.

prompt: A product's price was imported as the string `"79.90"`. Why does `find({ price: { $lt: NumberDecimal("100") } })` leave it out?

choices.text: Values compare by type first, and no string sits in a numeric range
choices.why: Right. The query does not fail; it returns a shorter list.

choices.text: The string is compared letter by letter, and "7" comes after "1" in that order
choices.why: A string is not compared with a number at all.

choices.text: The query raises a type error, which mongosh hides
choices.why: No error is raised; a find simply does not match across types.

choices.text: Strings are not indexed, so the query skips them
choices.why: There is no index here, and strings can be indexed.

prompt: Put these products in the order `find().sort({ price: 1 })` returns them.
hint: A missing field sorts like null; strings sort after numbers.
trap: The memory card is the cheapest and still comes last.

prompt: A developer types `db.prodcuts.insertOne(...)`. What does the server do?

choices.text: Refuses it, because `prodcuts` does not exist
choices.why: A first write creates the collection it names.

choices.text: Suggests `products` and waits for confirmation
choices.why: The server has no spelling suggestions.

choices.text: Writes the document into `products`, the closest name
choices.why: Names are matched exactly.

choices.text: Creates a collection called `prodcuts` and stores the document there
choices.why: Right, acknowledged: true. Only the list of collection names shows it.

prompt: You inherit a collection of 2 million orders and are told every `total` is a decimal. Which one query tests the claim and tells you how far it is wrong?

choices.text: `find({ total: { $type: "decimal" } }).count()`
choices.why: It counts the good ones and says nothing about which other types are there, missing included.

choices.text: `aggregate([{ $group: { _id: { $type: "$total" }, n: { $sum: 1 } } }])`
choices.why: Right. One row per type, missing included, with how many of each: the census.

choices.text: `findOne()`, read by a person
choices.why: One document proves nothing about two million.

choices.text: `find({ total: { $exists: false } })`
choices.why: That finds the missing ones only, not the strings or doubles.

prompt: A `$jsonSchema` validator is added with `collMod` to a collection where two documents already break it. What happens to those two?

choices.text: collMod is refused until they are fixed, naming both of them
choices.why: It answered { ok: 1 }; existing documents are not checked.

choices.text: They are deleted
choices.why: A validator never removes data.

choices.text: They stay, and the rule applies from the next write
choices.why: Right. Finding them is a $nor query around the validator.

choices.text: They are converted to the types the schema names
choices.why: Nothing is converted; the string price stayed a string until $set changed it.

prompt: Under `validationLevel: "strict"`, an update that only does `$inc: { stock: -1 }` is refused. Which document was it applied to?
hint: Strict checks the document the update leaves behind.

choices.text: One whose stock would have gone below zero
choices.why: That is possible, but the capture's refusal was about price, a field the update never touched.

choices.text: One already invalid elsewhere, such as a string price
choices.why: Right. Strict checks the whole resulting document; moderate lets updates to already-invalid documents through.

choices.text: One created before the validator existed, whatever it holds now
choices.why: A valid old document updates without trouble; age is not what is checked.

choices.text: Any document, because strict refuses every update
choices.why: Strict refuses only updates that leave an invalid document.

prompt: Match each validator setting to what an invalid write does under it.
hint: One behaviour belongs to none of them.

pairs.right: refused, with the failed rule in the error
accepted, and a line in the server's log
an update to an already-invalid document goes through

right_distractors: the document is fixed to match the schema

prompt: Put the steps of rolling a validator out on a busy collection in order.
items: read the log to learn which programs write invalid documents
repair the documents until the $nor census is empty
trap: Refusing first breaks the programs you have not found yet.

prompt: Which of these does a `$jsonSchema` validator on `products` give you? Choose every one that applies.

choices.text: An error at the moment a program writes a string price
choices.why: Yes, whichever program it is.

choices.text: A refusal of writes to a misspelt collection such as `prodcuts`
choices.why: The validator belongs to products; prodcuts is another collection with no rule.

choices.text: The details of which rule failed and the type it saw
choices.why: Yes: propertyName, specifiedAs, consideredType.

choices.text: A check of the documents stored before the rule existed
choices.why: Old documents are not checked; the $nor census is how you find them.

prompt: A report sums `total` across all orders and comes out a few cents off the accounting system. The totals are all numbers. What is the likeliest cause, given this lesson?

choices.text: Some totals are strings and were skipped by the sum
choices.why: The question says they are all numbers; a skipped string would be off by whole prices, not cents.

choices.text: The totals are doubles, and binary fractions do not add up to exact cents
choices.why: Right. Store money as Decimal128 built from strings, or as integer cents.

choices.text: Dates are in UTC, so a day's orders fall into the wrong report
choices.why: That would move whole orders between days, not cents across the total.

choices.text: ObjectIds sort by time, so the newest orders were not yet counted
choices.why: A sum does not depend on order, and these orders have integer ids.

prompt: Match each symptom to what most likely caused it.

pairs.right: its price is stored as a string

pairs.left: a product sorted before the cheapest one
pairs.right: its price field is misspelt, so price is missing
the filter names a document that does not exist

pairs.left: a stock of 10 after one restock of 5
